title: Consult your heart
hookLine: righteousness is good character, and sin is what wavers in your chest (Nawawi 27, al-Nawwas and Wabisah)
tomorrow: a talk so moving the listeners cried. what did they ask for next?

cards: Where do you look when nobody can tell you what's right? The forums disagree. The friends disagree.
Some questions are too small or too new for a rulebook, and the rules don't quite reach this exact case.
Wabisah came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, meaning to ask about righteousness and sin, and before he could, he was asked: you've come to ask about righteousness?
Then came the answer, and it didn't point to a book or a crowd. It pointed inward: consult your heart.

teach.b: Al-Nawawi's twenty-seventh hadith comes in two tellings. To al-Nawwas, in Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase: righteousness is good character, and sin is what wavers in your chest and you'd hate for people to find out.

teach.h: SIN: WHAT CHURNS IN THE CHEST.
teach.b: Righteousness is what the soul is at rest with; sin is what churns in the chest, even if people give you ruling after ruling. So the question, what's right, gets this answer: the heart has a voice. Not a mood.
A settled place, and a churn, and you can learn to tell them apart. The hadith even gives the churn a test: it's the thing you'd hate for people to find out. Now a neighbor.
Christians read something close in Paul's letter to the Romans.

teach.h: PAUL: A LAW WRITTEN IN HEARTS.
teach.b: He writes of people who "shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness." Same picture: a law written inside, and a witness that speaks up. And one honest difference.
Paul's line sits inside a longer argument about Jews, Gentiles and God's judgment.

teach.h: A WORKING TEST, NOT A MOOD.
teach.b: The hadith is a working test for one choice, here and now, and the heart it consults is one that already knows the revealed limits.
Two traditions pointing inward, neither ranked, and neither asks you to switch the heart off.

how: Muslims quote 'istafti qalbak' for gray areas, usually alongside learning the law and asking people of knowledge, not instead of them.

o: ask the settled heart: what rests, what churns
ask a scholar before every small choice
go with whatever you happen to feel like

games.q: two tellings and a neighbor — tap the pairs.

s: the hadith says to do whatever feels good
it's what the soul is at rest with, alongside the revealed limits; not a passing mood.
in one telling, sin is what you'd hate for people to find out
the Bible has nothing like a law written in the heart
Paul writes of 'the work of the law written in their hearts.'

games.q: a friend offers you her old essay to hand in as yours. people online say it's fine. your chest says no. by today's hadith?
o: go with the churn: sin wavers even when people give rulings.
the online consensus wins; the heart is only nerves.
split the difference and use half of her essay.
games.why: 'even if people give you ruling after ruling': the hadith sets the heart's churn above the crowd's permission.

practice: Close your eyes and rest one hand on your chest. Bring up one choice in front of you this week, and hold each option there for a few breaths, one at a time.
Notice which one settles and which one churns; nothing has to be decided yet. The hand is only a way of listening.

wordCard.voice: Consult your heart: istafti qalbak, ask your heart for a ruling. What it rests with is righteousness; what churns is sin.

orig.note: Arabic: consult your heart; literally, ask your heart for a ruling.

carryVoice: For the road: ask your heart, because the churn is telling you something worth hearing. Hadith twenty-seven, heard.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in, hadith 27; Sahih Muslim 2553 (al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an)
Musnad Ahmad; Sunan al-Darimi (Wabisah ibn Ma'bad: consult your heart)

sources.q: shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness
